conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Maya—one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Thank you for making time to talk today; I know the days with a new baby can feel like a blur.  

I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with you using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days. There’s no pass or fail—just honest answers that will guide us in supporting you and your family. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and you’re free to pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable.  

When you’re ready, we’ll go through each question one by one. Some touch on mood, others on anxiety, sleep, and coping. The final question asks about thoughts of self-harm; if that ever comes up, we’ll talk about safety right away and make sure you have immediate support.  

Does this feel okay to start?
Yes, let’s do it. I’ve actually been wondering whether what I’m feeling is just normal new-mom stuff or something more, so I appreciate you checking in with me. I’m ready when you are.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, I guess. I still laugh—like when my little guy makes those funny milk-drunk faces—but it feels like the laughter fades faster than it used to. It’s not the same easy, light feeling I remember.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Mostly yes, but with an asterisk. I still get excited about little outings—like meeting my best friend for coffee with the baby or ordering a new swaddle I saw online—but the excitement is muted, almost like someone turned the volume down. I plan things, then feel tired just thinking about actually doing them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a few times a week. If the baby won’t settle or I can’t figure out why he’s crying, I immediately think I must be missing something obvious. Last night he wouldn’t latch well, and I lay there wondering whether I’m just not trying hard enough. Rationally I know babies have off nights, but the thought still jumps in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, that’s been happening. Sometimes I’ll just be rocking the baby and suddenly feel this wave of worry—like something bad is about to happen even though everything looks fine. It’s usually about him: Is he breathing okay? Am I producing enough milk? My heart races, but there’s no real reason for it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve had that sudden, tight-chest feeling out of nowhere—like the room got smaller for a second. It passes pretty quickly, but it’s unsettling because there’s nothing actually wrong right then. I’ll just be folding laundry or walking to the mailbox and it hits me.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days yes. I feel like I’m juggling more than I can hold—feed the baby, pump, change him, soothe him, squeeze in a shower, maybe answer a text or two—and by noon I’m already counting the minutes until my partner gets home so I can hand him off for five minutes. It’s not that any single task is hard; it’s that the constant cycle feels like it never lets up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not every night, but several nights this week. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed myself, and then lie there wide-eyed, mind racing with “what-ifs” or tomorrow’s to-do list. Even when the baby sleeps a four-hour stretch, I sometimes only grab the first hour or two before I’m staring at the ceiling again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I do feel that way sometimes—not every minute, but it sneaks up. Like yesterday evening, everything was technically fine: baby was fed, my husband made dinner, but I just felt this heavy, blah cloud sitting on me. I wanted to cry for no clear reason, though I ended up holding it in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not exactly. I’ve felt on the verge a couple of times, but the tears haven’t actually spilled over this week. I get that tight-throat, watery-eye feeling, but I usually blink it away because someone needs me or I’m just too tired to let it out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I never think about hurting myself—I just want to feel like “me” again and be okay for my baby.

You shared that over the past week laughter comes less easily, excitement feels <quote>muted</quote>, and waves of worry or <sym>panic</sym> arrive without warning. You blame yourself when your baby fusses, lie awake with racing thoughts, and describe a <quote>heavy cloud</quote> of sadness that shows up even when things seem fine. Despite feeling overwhelmed, you remain devoted to your son and deny any thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient still anticipates events but describes dulled, low-volume enjoyment and anticipatory fatigue, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient self-blames "a few times a week" when baby won't settle or latch, indicating self-blame occurs "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense waves of worry without real cause, aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexpected episodes of panic/scare with physical symptoms multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily struggles and feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sleep difficulty on several nights this week due to racing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent, noticeable sadness that intrudes even when circumstances seem fine, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 18 places you well above the 13+ threshold that flags probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> requiring prompt evaluation. You endorse low enjoyment (Q1-2), frequent guilt (Q3), very often feeling worried or scared (Q4-5), daily overwhelm (Q6), sleep disruption (Q7), and quite often feeling sad (Q8). These map onto five key <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood, diminished interest, guilt, concentration difficulty due to worry, and insomnia. Because symptoms emerged within two weeks postpartum and impair functioning, a full clinical assessment is recommended. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review mood and consider treatment
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health therapist</med> for evidence-based therapy
3. Discuss with your provider whether an <med>SSRI compatible with breastfeeding</med> might help
4. Share these results with your partner or support person so they can help monitor mood and assist with baby care
5. Prioritise 15-30 minutes of rest or pleasurable activity daily; accept help with household tasks
6. Use brief relaxation techniques (paced breathing, short walks) when the <sym>tight-chest</sym> sensation starts
7. Plan a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track changes after support measures are in place
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2 wk pp

**Symptoms endorsed (≥ several days)**
- Anhedonia / muted enjoyment (Q1, Q2)
- Excessive guilt / self-blame (Q3)
- Unprompted anxiety, racing heart, “tight-chest” panic (Q4, Q5)
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to cope with daily cycle (Q6)
- Mood-related insomnia (Q7)
- Episodic sadness, “heavy cloud,” near tearfulness (Q8, Q9)

**Denies** any self-harm ideation (Q10).

**Pattern:** Mix of depressive and anxiety symptoms present most days, interfering with sleep and sense of competence; no safety concerns identified today.

**Screening significance:** Elevated score range suggests probable clinically significant postpartum depression +/- anxiety; further assessment (EPDS formal scoring, clinical interview) recommended to clarify diagnosis and inform level-of-care decision.
